29.title: Nine hundred and fifty years
29.hook: Nuh calls his people by night and by day, openly and in private, and few listen (71:5–9; 29:14)
29.howItsDone: Muslims honor Nuh as a prophet, and surah seventy-one, which bears his name, is read as a lesson in patient, persistent calling.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Habil, the brother who wouldn't raise his hand, and one life as all lives. Today, a man who kept talking for nine hundred and fifty years.
screen: `HABIL — ONE LIFE IS LIKE ALL LIVES.`

segments.voice: A teacher stands in front of a room where nobody's listening. Phones out, heads down, someone asleep in the back. She says it again, another way. Tries a joke. Tries a story. Stays after class in case anyone wants to ask. Almost nobody does. Now stretch that across many lifetimes. Nuh, Noah, is remembered for a boat. But the Qur'an spends whole passages on something else: how long he kept talking to people who wouldn't listen.
screen: `A ROOM WHERE NOBODY'S LISTENING.` → `SAY IT AGAIN, ANOTHER WAY.` → `NUH, BEFORE THE BOAT.`

segments.voice: A whole surah carries his name, surah seventy-one, and most of it is his own report to God. Paraphrasing: my Lord, I've called my people night and day, and my calling has only made them run further away. Every time I called them, so You could forgive them, they put their fingers in their ears and pulled their clothes over their heads. I called them openly. I spoke to them in public, and I spoke to them in private. Night and day, loud and quiet, crowds and one at a time: he tried everything. And what was he asking? Not much: ask your Lord's forgiveness; He is forgiving. He promised them rain, and gardens, and rivers. Then the number. In Pickthall's words, “he continued with them for a thousand years save fifty years.” Some scholars take it as it stands. Others note it describes how long he stayed among his people, and differ over how it fits his whole life. Either way, it's patience almost too long to imagine. And the result? The Qur'an is honest: only a few believed with him. By the world's measure, that looks like failure. But a hadith in Bukhari, about the Day of Judgment, has people coming to Nuh and calling him the first messenger to the people of the earth, and a grateful servant. His success wasn't counted in listeners. It was counted in the calling.

segments.voice: Sit quietly and say, slowly, the words Nuh asked of his people: I ask God's forgiveness. Give each word its own breath, and repeat it a few times without hurrying. If you don't pray, let the words be a simple wish to begin again.
Nuh. Noah: the prophet who called his people night and day for nine hundred and fifty years, while only a few listened.
Your line: call anyway. Few listened, and he never stopped calling. See you tomorrow.

30.title: Building on dry land
30.hook: Nuh builds the ark while his people mock him (11:37–38)
30.howItsDone: Muslims read the story of Nuh's ship in surah eleven and elsewhere, and draw from it steadiness in doing right when others mock.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Nuh, calling his people night and day, and your line, call anyway. Today, he puts down the words and picks up a hammer.

A man far from any sea is sawing planks in the sun, day after day. He's building a ship. Not a little boat for a river: a ship, on dry land. People on their way to the market slow down to stare. Some shake their heads. Some laugh out loud. A few shout something clever, and their friends laugh too. The Qur'an never says where, so let the scene stay simple: one man, one hammer, and a crowd.
screen: `A SHIP IN A DRY VALLEY.` → `PEOPLE STOP TO LAUGH.` → `NUH PICKS UP A HAMMER.`

segments.voice: Surah eleven. After all those years of calling, God tells Nuh that no more of his people will believe beyond those who already have. Don't grieve over what they do. Then the instruction, in Pickthall's words: “Build the ship under Our eyes and by Our inspiration.” Under Our eyes: commentators explain it as watched over, guarded, in Our care. He isn't building alone, even if it looks that way from the road. The next verse brings the crowd. Every time the leaders of his people passed by, they mocked him. The verse doesn't record their jokes, only his answer. Paraphrasing: if you laugh at us now, we'll laugh at you in the same way, and soon you'll know. It's not a curse. It's a man who's sure of the weather. Another surah gives a plain detail: the ship was a thing of planks and nails. No miracle wood, just ordinary carpentry, done by hand. When it's finished, the sign comes: the oven gushes. Commentators differ over what that means, an actual oven, or the face of the earth bursting with water. And God tells him to load a pair of every kind, his family, and those who believe. Nuh builds before there's a cloud in the sky, because when the rain comes, it's too late to start. Doing the right thing often looks foolish, right up to the day it doesn't. He didn't need the crowd to understand. He needed the ship to be ready.

segments.voice: Sit still and bring to mind one right thing you do that might look odd to others: a prayer at work, a fast, a quiet no. Hold it calmly, and let three words from the verse settle with each breath: under Our eyes. Then let the picture go.
Al-fulk, the ship: what Nuh built under God's eyes, plank by plank on dry land, while his people laughed.
Your line: build before the rain. The ship was ready before the first cloud. Day thirty, done.

31.title: The son on the mountain
31.hook: Nuh's own son refuses the ark, says a mountain will save him, and the waves come between them (11:42–43)
31.howItsDone: Muslims read Nuh's call to his son in surah eleven, and many parents recall it when a child has turned away: faith can't be handed down, but a parent keeps praying.

segments.voice: Yesterday: al-fulk, the ship Nuh built on dry land while the town laughed. Today the ship is afloat, and the story narrows to one face.

Waves like mountains, the Qur'an says. A ship rides them, carrying the few who believed. And from the deck, a father sees his son, standing apart, as the water rises. Many families have someone like that son. The one you can't reach. The brother who stopped answering. The daughter who moved across the country and calls twice a year. You love them, you've tried everything, and they're still on the other side of something you can't cross.
screen: `WAVES LIKE MOUNTAINS.` → `ONE FACE, AS THE WATER RISES.` → `THE ONE YOU CAN'T REACH.`

segments.voice: Surah eleven. Nuh calls to his son, in Pickthall's words: “O my son! Come ride with us.” After nine hundred and fifty years of calling his own people, the last call in the story is a father calling his child. The son answers, paraphrasing: I'll go up a mountain; it will keep me safe from the water. He trusts the highest thing he can see. Nuh answers: today nothing can protect from God's command, except the one He has mercy on. Then one of the saddest lines in the Qur'an: “And the wave came in between them.” No speech. A wave, between a father and a son. The Qur'an doesn't name the son; tradition calls him Kan'an. But it doesn't end there. When the water settles and the ship rests on a mountain called al-Judi, Nuh turns to God. Paraphrasing: my Lord, my son was of my family, and Your promise is true. He's still calling. God answers gently but firmly: he is not of your family, his conduct was not right; don't ask Me about what you don't know. And Nuh asks forgiveness for even asking. Many commentators say family, in this answer, means the family of faith, not blood. What everyone notices is the father: a prophet who could accept anything from God, still reaching for his son, right to the end.

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you can't reach right now: far away, estranged, or just closed off. Don't rehearse the argument; just hold their face for a few breaths. If you pray, pray for them in your own words, the way Nuh kept asking for his son; if you don't, wish them well, silently, as if across water.
Kan'an, the name tradition gives Nuh's son, who trusted a mountain over the ship, and was lost in the wave.
Your line: a father still calls. Even after the wave, Nuh was still asking for his son. That's day thirty-one.

32.title: Star, moon, sun
32.hook: the young Ibrahim watches a star, the moon, the sun set, and says he will not love what sets (6:76–79)
32.howItsDone: Muslims call Ibrahim hanif, upright, and the model of pure faith; the Qur'an tells Muslims to follow the religion of Ibrahim, and a blessing recited near the end of the prayer names him.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Kan'an, the son on the mountain, and the wave that came between him and his father. Today, a new prophet, and a night sky.

Lie on your back somewhere dark, far from the city. The first star comes out, so bright you'd swear it was a plane. Later the moon rises, huge and orange, and the star looks small. In the morning the sun swallows them both. By evening, the sun is gone too. Long ago, a young man watched that same sky and asked a question. His name was Ibrahim, Abraham, a prophet honored by Jews, Christians and Muslims alike.
screen: `THE FIRST STAR, SO BRIGHT.` → `THE MOON, THEN THE SUN.` → `A YOUNG MAN LOOKING UP.`

segments.voice: Surah six. Ibrahim lives among people who worship idols and the lights of the sky. Night falls, and he sees a star. This is my Lord, he says. Then the star sets, and he says, in Pickthall's words: “I love not things that set.” The moon rises, brighter: this is my Lord. The moon sets. Then the sun, blazing: this is my Lord, this one is greater. And the sun goes down too. So he turns away from all of it, toward the One who made the heavens and the earth, as one by nature upright. The Arabic word is hanif: the one who leans toward God, and away from everything else. Scholars read this scene two ways, and both are old. Some say it's a young man truly searching, trying each light in turn, until he sees that anything that disappears can't be God. Others point to the verses around it. His people worshipped the stars, and Ibrahim, they say, already knew. He was walking them through their own logic out loud, star by star, so they could hear where it led. Either way, his test is simple enough for a child. Does it set? Does it fade, or leave, or go dark? Then it can't be the thing you give your whole heart to. His word for things that set, afilin, also means things that fade and vanish. It's a question you can ask of almost anything you love too much.
screen: `A STAR, AND IT SETS.` · `THE MOON, THE SUN: GONE TOO.` · `SEARCHING, OR TEACHING?` · `HANIF — LEANING TOWARD GOD.` · then, large: `I LOVE NOT THINGS THAT SET.`

segments.voice: If you can, look out a window at the sky, day or night; if not, picture the last sky you saw. Watch the light for a few slow breaths, and notice that even up there, things are moving. If you pray, turn your face, as Ibrahim did, toward the One who made it all.
Star. The first light Ibrahim saw set, then the moon, then the sun, and he said: I love not things that set.
Your line: love what doesn't set. Ibrahim's whole test fits in three words: does it set? See you tomorrow.

33.title: The idols and the axe
33.hook: Ibrahim breaks his people's idols and leaves the biggest one standing with the axe (21:57–58)
33.howItsDone: Muslims tell the story of Ibrahim and the idols to children as a lesson in thinking for oneself and in tawhid, and it's read in surahs twenty-one and thirty-seven.

segments.voice: Yesterday: star, moon and sun, and Ibrahim's test, does it set? Today he takes that question indoors, to his own people's idols.

A row of carved figures in a temple, and a young man staring at them. Ibrahim asks his people why they worship them, and gets an answer you may have heard at home: that's how we've always done it. The Thanksgiving dish nobody actually likes. The route to Grandma's that takes twenty minutes longer. The way we just don't talk about Uncle Ray. It takes a certain kind of person to keep asking why after that. Usually a kid. And this time, Ibrahim doesn't stop at asking.
screen: `A ROW OF CARVED FIGURES.` → `THAT'S HOW WE'VE ALWAYS DONE IT.` → `A KID WHO KEEPS ASKING WHY.`

segments.voice: Surah twenty-one. Ibrahim says to his father and his people, in Pickthall's words: “What are these images unto which ye pay devotion?” Their answer, paraphrasing: we found our fathers worshipping them. That's the whole reason. Ibrahim says: then you and your fathers have been plainly wrong. And he makes a promise: by God, I'll deal with your idols once you've turned your backs and gone. The commentators say the whole town went out to a festival. While the temple stood empty, he broke the idols into pieces, in Pickthall's words, “all save the chief of them.” He left the biggest one standing, the verse says, so that they might turn to it. And the axe? The Qur'an never mentions one. It comes from the commentators' retelling, which says Ibrahim hung the axe on the big idol, or put it in its hand, as if to say: ask him. A vivid detail, and it's tradition, not the verse. What the verse does give is the trap: a room of smashed statues, and one big one left untouched. When the town comes back, they'll have to decide what they believe that big one can do. Ibrahim hasn't made a speech. He's made a question they can't avoid. Sometimes the kindest way to break a habit isn't to argue about it. It's to let the habit answer for itself.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you do only because you've always done it. Hold it up the way Ibrahim looked at the row of images, and ask it plainly: why are you here, and what can you actually do? If you pray, ask for clear eyes.
Ibrahim. He broke his people's idols, left the biggest one standing, and let it wait for their questions.
Your line: ask the big one. Ibrahim left one idol standing so the question would stay in the room. Day thirty-three, done.

34.title: "Ask them, if they can speak"
34.hook: the people accuse him, and he tells them to ask the idols, and they fall silent (21:62–65)
34.howItsDone: Muslims read Ibrahim's questioning of the idols as a model of patient reasoning, and teachers use his words to invite people to think honestly about what they rely on.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ibrahim broke the idols and left the biggest one standing. Your line was ask the big one. Today, the town asks him.

The festival is over, and the town comes home. Someone walks into the temple and stops dead. Pieces everywhere: heads on the floor, arms snapped off. And in the middle of the wreckage, the biggest idol, untouched, standing tall. Who did this to our gods? Word goes around about a young man who's been talking about them. His name is Ibrahim. Bring him out, they say, in front of everyone. They ask him straight out, and his answer turns the question around.
screen: `THE TOWN COMES HOME.` → `WHO DID THIS TO OUR GODS?` → `BRING HIM OUT, IN FRONT OF EVERYONE.`

segments.voice: Surah twenty-one. They ask: Ibrahim, was it you who did this to our gods? He points at the big one. In Pickthall's words: “But this, their chief hath done it. So question them, if they can speak.” And the crowd goes quiet. The Qur'an says they turned to one another, and to themselves, and said: surely it's you who are the wrongdoers. A real moment of honesty. For one breath, the whole town sees it: statues that can't say who broke them can't hear a prayer either. Then the next verse says, literally, that they were turned back onto their heads. The old thinking came flooding back, and they said to him: “Well thou knowest that these speak not.” Listen to what they just admitted. Ibrahim asks: then do you worship, instead of God, what can neither help you nor harm you? So was his answer, their chief did it, a lie? A hadith in Bukhari counts it among three times Ibrahim said something not literally true, and says two of them, this one included, were for God's sake. Scholars explain it as a pointed kind of irony, said so the listeners would work out for themselves that it couldn't be true. The moment you say it can't speak, you've answered your own question. Ibrahim didn't win an argument. He let them hear themselves say it.

35.title: The fire made cool
35.hook: they throw Ibrahim into a great fire and Allah says, fire, be cool and safe for him (21:68–69)
35.howItsDone: Many Muslims say hasbuna llahu wa ni'ma l-wakil, God is enough for us and the best one to trust, in moments of fear, remembering Ibrahim in the fire.

segments.voice: Yesterday: ask them, if they can speak. The town admitted it. Your line was they cannot speak. Today, the town answers back.

A crowd embarrassed in front of itself doesn't always change its mind. Sometimes it gets angry. This week has been full of people who paid for speaking up. Nuh, calling for nine hundred and fifty years, building a ship on dry land while people laughed, calling to his son as the wave came between them. Ibrahim, watching the star set, breaking the idols, letting the town hear itself say: they cannot speak. Nuh was mocked. Ibrahim is about to find out what it costs. This crowd builds a fire.
screen: `A CROWD, EMBARRASSED.` → `A WEEK OF SPEAKING UP.` → `AND THEY BUILD A FIRE.`

segments.voice: Surah twenty-one. The crowd has lost the argument, so they reach for the only thing left. In Pickthall's words: “Burn him and stand by your gods, if ye will be doing.” The commentators' retellings make the fire enormous: wood gathered for days, a blaze so hot that birds flying over it fell, Ibrahim thrown in from a distance by a kind of catapult. Those details are tradition; the Qur'an doesn't give them. What it gives is one sentence, God speaking to the fire itself: “O fire, be coolness and peace for Abraham.” In Arabic, bardan wa salaman. Cool, and safe. And the fire obeys. The commentators preserve an old observation: if God had said only be cool, the fire might have frozen him. So He said cool, and safe. Exactly enough. What was Ibrahim doing as he fell? A report in Bukhari, from Ibn Abbas, says his words were: hasbuna llahu wa ni'ma l-wakil. God is enough for us, and the best one to trust. The same words, the report says, were later said by the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and his companions when they were told an army was gathering against them. The line is still said today in moments of fear. Notice the order. Ibrahim didn't wait to see whether the fire would cool before he trusted. The trust came first, in midair. The coolness came after. And the verse doesn't say the fire went out. It says what the fire was told to be.
